This is an architectural boundary, not a claim that Redis is not a database or cannot persist data. Redis supports optional persistence, but persistence alone does not determine which system is authoritative.

The key was warm when I took it from the envelope.

I stood on the landing and turned it over in my palm. Brass, ordinary teeth, a smear of green near the bow. There was no apartment number on the door. The other doors in the building had numbers, peepholes, little signs asking delivery drivers not to knock. This one had a brass handle and, near the bottom, a shallow dent shaped like the toe of a shoe.

Downstairs, someone laughed. A pipe clicked inside the wall.

I checked the envelope again. My name was written on the front in blue ink. Nothing else.

“You’ve got the wrong person,” I said, quietly, to whoever had left it.

Then I put the key in the lock.

It resisted at first. I drew it back a fraction, lifted the handle, tried again. The small adjustments came easily, though I couldn’t have said why I thought they would help.

The lock turned.

I kept my hand on the key. On the other side, something scraped across the floor, then stopped.

“Hello?”

No answer.

I pushed the door a few inches. Its lower edge caught on a rug. Through the gap I could see a strip of yellow wallpaper, a coat hook, the curved end of an umbrella handle.

The smell reached me before I got my shoulder against the wood: boiled potatoes, furniture polish, and the faint scorched smell of an iron left resting on cloth.

I pushed harder. The rug folded beneath the door.

There was a kitchen at the end of the hall. Afternoon light lay across the table, although the landing window behind me had been dark. A cup stood beside a plate of bread and butter. One slice had a bite taken out of it.

I stepped inside.

My shoes sounded too loud on the floorboards. I found myself placing my feet along the runner, avoiding the bare wood, and stopped when I noticed what I was doing.

On the coat hook hung a small red jacket. One cuff had been repaired with brown thread.

I touched the sleeve. The lining was cool beneath my finger.

From the kitchen came the soft clink of a spoon against a cup.

“Leave that open,” a woman said. “I’m trying to get some air through.”

I looked back at the unfamiliar door. There was a bolt on this side, high enough that a child couldn’t reach it.

“Who are you?” I asked.

A chair moved. I waited for someone to appear in the kitchen doorway, but no one did.

“Your tea’s getting cold.”

I had heard that voice for years on a cassette my father kept in his bedside drawer. It was younger here, clearer without the hiss of the tape.

I let go of the jacket.

“Mom?”

The spoon stopped.

Then, very slowly, I pushed the door all the way open.
